html:
The Belgian Congo was Belgium's colony in central Africa, covering the Congo basin, from 1908 to 1960. The map shows it in 1914 and 1938. It is today the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

It was born from scandal. King Leopold II had ruled the Congo Free State as his own property, and the forced labour, killings and mutilations of the rubber regime caused an international outcry led by the Congo Reform Association. In 1908 the Belgian state took the colony over.

Belgium ran it through a partnership of state, Catholic missions and big companies. Copper from Katanga, mined by Union Miniere, made it one of Africa's richest colonies. Uranium from its Shinkolobwe mine went into the first American atomic bombs. Africans were given primary schools and clinics but almost no higher education and no political voice.

When independence came suddenly in June 1960, under Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba, the new state fell at once into crisis. From 1971 it was called Zaire.
